notes.meaning: Isaiah introduces a heavy message from God announcing the future fall of Babylon. A 'burden' in Scripture is a weighty prophecy that warns of coming judgment. God gave this message long before Babylon grew into a mighty empire, so His people would take comfort knowing He rules over every world power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historical critics argue that Isaiah did not write this chapter because Babylon was not yet the dominant world empire in his day, suggesting it was written by an author living during the exile.

notes.meaning: God commands a signal flag to be raised on a bare, treeless mountain where everyone can see it. War heralds are told to shout and wave their hands to summon an attacking army. This army will march straight into the stately gates of Babylon's proud rulers.

The Lord calls the invading soldiers His 'sanctified ones,' which means they are set apart for His special assignment rather than morally holy. He gives these warriors strength to carry out His righteous anger against Babylon. Even though the invaders seek their own conquest, God uses their fierce pride to accomplish His divine plan.

A loud roar echoes across the distant mountains as many nations gather for war. This sound comes from a massive alliance brought together to attack the empire. The Lord of hosts is Himself assembling and directing these battle forces.

The attacking armies come from remote lands at the edges of the known world. They are the instruments and weapons God uses to pour out His just anger. Through them, the Lord will bring devastation across the whole Babylonian land.

The people of Babylon are told to wail because the Day of the Lord is fast approaching. This day refers to a special season when God steps in to judge evil and set things right. Because the disaster comes directly from the Almighty, no human power will be able to stop it.

Terror will completely paralyze the defenders of the city. Their hands will hang down limp and useless, unable to hold weapons or fight back. Every heart will melt in sheer helplessness before God's judgment.

Agony and sudden panic will seize the people like the sharp labor pains of childbirth. Citizens will stare at one another in speechless shock as their defenses collapse. Their faces will burn hot and flushed from extreme distress and dread.

The Day of the Lord brings unsparing judgment upon stubborn evildoers. It is called 'cruel' not because God is wicked, but because His fierce justice feels harsh and painful to those who rebel against Him. The land will be stripped bare, and the sinners who practiced evil within it will be destroyed.

Darkness will cover the sky as the sun, moon, and stars withhold their light. In the language of the prophets, celestial darkness often paints a vivid picture of political chaos, the collapse of governments, and the total loss of earthly hope. God's withdrawal of light shows that His favor has turned away from the city.

differ.view: These cosmic signs describe literal physical changes in the sun, moon, and stars that will happen during the final tribulation before Christ returns.

notes.meaning: God declares that He will bring punishment on the empire for its wicked deeds and oppression. Babylon is called 'the world' because its vast dominion felt like the whole earth to the people of that day. The Lord specifically targets the arrogant pride and ruthless cruelty of its rulers.

The coming slaughter will be so sweeping that surviving men will become exceedingly rare. Human beings will be harder to find than pure gold from Ophir, which was famous for its quality. The attackers will desire blood rather than money, refusing to spare any life for a ransom.

God's fierce anger is described as an earthquake that shakes the heavens and wrenches the earth from its foundations. This poetic imagery illustrates the total upheaval and ruin of the Babylonian kingdom. It reminds us that only God's kingdom cannot be moved when world powers crumble.

Foreign soldiers and traders in Babylon will flee in total panic, like terrified gazelles fleeing hunters or sheep without a shepherd. They will abandon the collapsing city and run back to their own homelands. No foreign alliances will be able to protect Babylon from its downfall.

Anyone left behind in the fallen city will be run through with the sword, and retreating troops will be cut down. The conquerors will carry out the brutal warfare common to the ancient world, plundering homes, harming women, and slaying infants before the eyes of their parents. God permits these horrors to fall on Babylon as repayment for the cruelties it had inflicted on other nations.

The Lord expressly names the Medes as the power He will send against Babylon. They will be driven by a fierce desire for conquest rather than money, refusing to accept gold or silver to spare captives. God's ability to name specific nations centuries ahead demonstrates His complete mastery over world events.

The invaders will use large, powerful bows to shoot down the young defenders of the city. They will show no pity to the innocent, slaying even unborn babies and little children. This portrays the terrible brutality of unbridled warfare when God removes His protection.

Babylon was the jewel and crown of the Chaldean empire, celebrated across the ancient world for its beauty and mighty walls. Yet God announces that it will end up like Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed by divine judgment. Although its decline occurred gradually across centuries after its capture, the ruin proved just as complete and permanent.

differ.view: Because ancient Babylon was captured without being instantly incinerated like Sodom, this prophecy requires a future rebuilt city of Babylon to be cataclysmically destroyed at the end of time.

notes.meaning: Once destroyed, Babylon will never again be rebuilt or lived in from age to age. The land will be so desolate that wandering desert nomads will not even pitch their tents there, nor will shepherds graze their flocks on its ruined soil. History records that the site became an empty wasteland, fulfilling this word to the letter.

Wild desert beasts, screeching owls, ostriches, and howling jackals will make their homes in Babylon's crumbling palaces and luxurious gardens. Frightful creatures will wander through the grand fortresses where emperors once feasted. God warns that Babylon's appointed time of judgment is certain and will not be delayed.
